content: Human embryogenesis is the intricate process of cell division and cellular differentiation that occurs in the human embryo during the early stages of prenatal development. This process begins at the moment of fertilization and continues until the end of the 8th week of gestational age, after which the developing organism is referred to as a fetus. A human begins as a single cell called a zygote, which is formed when an ovum (egg) is fertilized by a single spermatozoon (sperm). The zygote is encased in a robust glycoprotein membrane known as the zona pellucida, which the successful sperm has penetrated. The zygote undergoes a series of mitotic divisions, known as cleavage, increasing the number of cells while remaining within the confines of the zona pellucida. After the 8-cell stage, the cells undergo compaction, a process where they adhere tightly to one another, forming a compact sphere. At this point, the embryo is referred to as a morula, which consists of approximately 16 cells. Following compaction, cavitation occurs. During this process, the outermost layer of cells, called the trophoblast, secretes fluid into the morula, leading to the formation of a central, fluid-filled cavity known as the blastocoel. When the cell count reaches approximately 40 to 150, the zona pellucida begins to degenerate, allowing the embryo to expand in volume. This stage, reached around four to six days after fertilization, is known as the blastocyst stage. The blastocyst stage persists until implantation in the uterine wall. The blastocyst is characterized by two distinct groups of cells: the inner cell mass (also called the embryoblast) and the trophoblast. The inner cell mass will develop into the embryo proper, as well as the amnion, yolk sac, and allantois, while the trophoblast will eventually form the placenta. Structurally, the blastocyst resembles a hollow ball of trophoblast cells, with the inner cell mass attached to the inner wall of this ball. At this stage, the embryo and its associated membranes are collectively referred to as the conceptus, which is now located within the uterus. The zona pellucida completely disappears, enabling the blastocyst to invade the endometrium (the innermost epithelial lining of the uterus) and initiate implantation. During implantation, the trophoblast differentiates into two distinct layers. The inner layer, known as the cytotrophoblast, consists of cuboidal cells that serve as the source of dividing cells. The outer layer, called the syncytiotrophoblast, facilitates the implantation of the blastocyst into the endometrium by forming finger-like projections called chorionic villi. These villi penetrate the uterine lining and create spaces, known as lacunae, which fill with maternal blood. This process is aided by hydrolytic enzymes that erode the uterine epithelium. The syncytiotrophoblast also produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a hormone that signals the maternal body of pregnancy and prevents menstruation by maintaining the corpus luteum. The chorionic villi begin to branch and develop fetal blood vessels, enabling gas exchange between the mother and the developing embryo. While the syncytiotrophoblast invades the uterine wall, the inner cell mass (embryoblast) undergoes further development. The embryoblast forms a bilaminar embryonic disc, composed of two layers: the epiblast and the hypoblast. The epiblast, adjacent to the trophoblast, consists of columnar cells, while the hypoblast, closer to the blastocyst cavity, is made up of cuboidal cells. The epiblast, now referred to as the primitive ectoderm, will undergo gastrulation around day 16 post-fertilization, giving rise to the three germ layers of the embryo: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The hypoblast, or primitive endoderm, contributes only to extraembryonic structures, such as the lining of the primary yolk sac. The epiblast separates from the trophoblast to form a new cavity, the amniotic cavity, which is lined by the amniotic membrane. This membrane is composed of cells derived from the epiblast, known as amnioblasts. Meanwhile, some hypoblast cells migrate along the inner lining of the cytotrophoblast, secreting an extracellular matrix to form Heuser's membrane (or the exocoelomic membrane). The blastocoel is now referred to as the primary yolk sac (or exocoelomic cavity). Cytotrophoblast cells and Heuser's membrane cells continue to secrete extracellular matrix material, forming the extraembryonic reticulum. Epiblast cells migrate along the outer edges of this reticulum, forming the extraembryonic mesoderm, which eventually disrupts the reticulum. Pockets form within the reticulum, coalescing to create the chorionic cavity (or extraembryonic coelom). A new layer of cells migrates from the hypoblast along the inside of the primary yolk sac, pushing it to the abembryonic pole of the embryo and forming a new cavity, the secondary or definitive yolk sac. The remnants of the primary yolk sac are referred to as exocoelomic vesicles. Exposure to toxic substances during the first two weeks following fertilization (corresponding to the second and third weeks of gestational age) may result in prenatal death but does not typically cause developmental defects. Instead, the body often responds with a miscarriage. However, toxic exposures during the embryonic period can lead to significant congenital malformations, as this is the critical time when the precursors of major organ systems are forming.
